text:
Imagine a public benefits office buys an AI tool to help process applications. The system performs well in demonstrations, but it misreads documents in a language widely spoken in the country. Staff start seeing delays, families miss payments, and the vendor has information that could help explain what went wrong. Another government may already be considering the same tool with no way to find out about the failure.

I support Lana Nusseibeh for UN Secretary-General because her programme identifies where countries could start cooperating. She proposes voluntary incident reporting, shared tests for the most powerful systems and wider participation by countries that use these technologies but have little influence over how they’re developed or evaluated.

Governments will differ on how they regulate AI. They can still agree on what information to share after a serious failure, how to protect the people affected when reporting it and what evidence to ask for before using a system in an essential service. Shared testing could also reveal where strong average scores hide consistent failures in particular languages or settings.

That’s where wider participation makes a difference. A country whose public services operate in several languages should be able to help decide what gets tested. A government with limited technical staff should be able to learn from another country’s experience before signing a contract. And when a tool causes harm, the people who rely on that service should have a way to get the decision reviewed.

I back Nusseibeh because I want the UN to help countries ask these questions together. A family waiting on a benefits payment should be able to count on the system working in their language and on someone being able to fix the mistake when it doesn’t.

text:
The Political Battle Over AI and The Fight To Control America’s Economic Future Before 2028

On September 13, I examined the convergence of political interests, corporate incentives and calls to slow AI development. On November 3, I discussed how an economic crisis could reshape AI policy. On November 11, I questioned the timing of the intelligence revelations surrounding Jensen Huang.

Following Huang’s reinstatement, Hakeem Jeffries is demanding investigations into NVIDIA, Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce, alongside stronger semiconductor export restrictions.

The Political Groundwork

In December 2025, Jeffries established the House Democratic Commission on AI and the Innovation Economy.

In September, Obama privately encouraged making AI central to the Democratic agenda, while Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Elon Musk expressed support for stronger AI oversight.

Democrats had reason to anticipate a strong midterm performance and develop their governing agenda before assuming congressional control.

On October 29, Democratic lawmakers introduced a resolution opposing taxpayer bailouts following an AI collapse. Valerie Foushee, a leader of Jeffries’s AI commission, was a sponsor.

That same day, the Huang intelligence revelations became public, 5 days before the midterms.

The Intelligence Disclosure

Trump was reportedly briefed in 2025, while Rubio oversaw an intelligence assessment in spring 2026.

My post examined 2 possibilities.

•    Individuals with access to classified intelligence strategically disclosed the information for political leverage.

•    Chinese intelligence sacrificed a potentially compromised relationship to destabilize American AI leadership and semiconductor policy.

Neither theory has been established. Why intelligence reportedly known for months surfaced immediately before the election deserves scrutiny.

Democrats subsequently secured a decisive electoral victory and will gain greater congressional investigative authority in January.

The Economic And Political Collision

Huang’s resignation intensified technology losses and institutional deleveraging. His reinstatement restored approximately $950 billion in NVIDIA market capitalization.

Persistent energy disruptions threaten corporate profitability and household purchasing power. Credit conditions are deteriorating while AI infrastructure commitments face uncertainty surrounding future returns.

Congressional investigations could examine AI financing, private credit, export licensing, electricity costs, corporate relationships and employment displacement.

Established AI companies could benefit from regulatory requirements that smaller competitors struggle to afford.

Political and corporate interests could therefore converge around the same regulatory agenda without any coordinated effort to engineer a market collapse.

The Battle Over What Comes After

If a severe recession develops in 2027, disagreements over corporate bailouts, household relief, AI regulation and responsibility for economic losses could dominate Washington.

Democratic congressional control could influence that response.

Persistent energy inflation could delay monetary easing. Even when rate cuts begin, monetary policy cannot restore energy supplies or make unprofitable AI investments economically viable.

The broader benefits for employment, consumption and investment could take 18 to 24 months or longer to materialize.

If easing begins in 2027, meaningful recovery might not arrive until 2028 or 2029, carrying significant electoral consequences.

Politicians do not need to manufacture an economic crisis to influence its consequences. Huang’s reinstatement may have temporarily stabilized the AI trade, but the larger battle over who regulates the industry, who absorbs its potential losses and who receives credit for the eventual economic recovery may only be beginning.

text:
🇺🇲 America's governors just told Congress how to regulate AI. Washington gets the most powerful models, the states keep everything else, and any attempt to override them will face a fight

A bipartisan group of US governors on Sunday published its blueprint for dividing AI regulation between Washington and the states, a direct message to the Congress that takes power in January.

The National Governors Association's Governors Council to Secure American AI Dominance is led by Maryland's Wes Moore and North Carolina's Josh Stein, both Democrats, and Republicans Mike Braun of Indiana and Spencer Cox of Utah. Its principles ask the federal government to enact a risk-based framework for frontier models, the most advanced general-purpose systems "whose risks and reach are national in scale." Those models should be evaluated or audited by independent experts, and developers should have to report security breaches and significant safety incidents to federal authorities and affected states.

Washington would also set national standards for AI threats to critical infrastructure, including financial systems, chemical, biological and nuclear security, and cybersecurity. And it should lead international talks on AI standards, trade and security.

The states would keep a long list. Governors want to remain "a primary accountability mechanism" for AI harms to consumers, and to protect children from addictive design, chatbots and companion apps. They also claim oversight of AI scams aimed at older people, automated decisions on housing, jobs, lending and insurance, and AI use in state government.

The sharpest line is on preemption, the idea that a federal law could wipe out state AI rules. The governors say any such move should be "approached cautiously" with input from a "representative cross-section of states," and that they will judge it against their own federalism principles. That is a warning to Republicans in Congress. A bipartisan House draft from Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan, released in June, would preempt state laws "specifically regulating the development" of AI models for three years, according to Roll Call. Safety groups called that a "generational mistake."

"We agree that humans must stay in control, and we must protect our people," Moore said. Cox argued that "we don't have to choose between innovation and safety." Stein said the risks are "too big to ignore."

For AI companies hoping one federal law would end the patchwork of state rules, governors from both parties have just said they intend to stay at the table.

name: Fundamental Notes
bio: Fundamental analysis in plain English. Financial statements, business models and valuation, explained through real company examples.
text:
How much of Amazon’s AI infrastructure build has already been paid for, and how much depends on future cash? I would start with that question before treating either AWS growth or a large commitments table as the whole answer. Its Q3 statements show a profitable cloud business, heavy company-wide equipment spending, substantial recorded borrowing and agreements that will be paid over several years.

AWS generated $46.0 billion of Q3 sales, up 39% from a year earlier, and $17.8 billion of operating income, up from $11.4 billion. Operating income is sales after the costs Amazon assigns to running that segment, before interest and taxes. The result supports a clear judgment: current cloud demand is reaching reported profit. AWS includes services beyond AI, and Amazon does not publish a separate profit figure for AI workloads. The segment result cannot establish the return on every new data center.

Follow the cash first

Amazon generated $42.4 billion of consolidated operating cash flow in Q3, compared with $35.5 billion a year earlier. Cash capital expenditures were $75.9 billion, up from $34.2 billion. These cash purchases primarily support technology infrastructure, most of it for AWS growth, as well as fulfillment capacity. I would keep the company-wide label attached: the filing does not allocate every dollar of that spending to AI.

For the trailing twelve months, operating cash flow was $168.3 billion. Purchases of property and equipment, net of sale proceeds and incentives, were $210.657 billion. My math: subtracting the second figure from the first gives negative $42.357 billion, matching Amazon’s definition of free cash flow. A negative result says the current build absorbed more cash than operations generated over that period. It does not say the equipment produced no revenue, and it does not measure its lifetime return.

The cash statement also has a timing limit. Amazon reports that the nine-month increase in property and equipment acquired but not yet paid was $21.473 billion. Some received technology assets can sit in accounts payable under payment terms of up to a year. Their cash purchase appears when Amazon pays the supplier. So I would check both cash capital expenditure and unpaid equipment next quarter; either one alone can make the pace of the build look smoother than it is.

What is recorded today

At September 30, Amazon reported $55.783 billion of cash and cash equivalents and $58.443 billion of marketable securities. Its filing identifies $2.931 billion of restricted cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities separately; funds pledged or otherwise restricted are not freely available for every purpose. Long-term debt stood at $173.125 billion, up from $65.648 billion at year-end 2025. Q3 interest expense rose to $1.7 billion from $538 million. Those are current balance-sheet and income-statement effects of financing, not estimates of future borrowing.

Commenced leases are another recorded obligation. Amazon reports a $114.783 billion present value of operating and finance lease liabilities at September 30. Present value discounts future payments to a balance-sheet amount. The contractual payment schedule, which includes interest, is larger. Treating both figures as separate bills and adding them would count the same leases twice.

What has yet to start

The filing lists $164.922 billion of future payments for leases that had not commenced at September 30. A lease can be signed while a facility is still under construction. Those future payments are disclosed in the commitments note, while the related lease has not reached the same balance-sheet stage as a commenced lease. The figure spans future years and multiple facilities; it is not a Q4 cash payment or an AI-only total.

Amazon also lists $159.640 billion of property-and-equipment purchase obligations. The note says these include long-term agreements that are not reflected on the balance sheet. The schedule includes $63.900 billion for 2027, but that is a contractual payment schedule, not a forecast of all 2027 capital spending. Purchases outside the listed agreements and changes in delivery timing can alter actual cash outlays. Some agreements with variable prices are included only to the extent of a minimum amount.

The commitments table totals $883.581 billion across debt principal and interest, leases, equipment purchases, other unconditional purchases and other obligations. I would not call that Amazon’s remaining AI bill. It combines financing for assets already acquired with payments for future assets, includes retail and media-related obligations, and runs well beyond next year. The table is useful because it tells us what kinds of claims on cash exist and when they are scheduled. Its grand total does not answer how much incremental AI spending remains.

Two sensitivities show the cash question without pretending to forecast 2027. My math: if operating cash flow were 20% above the last twelve months while net equipment cash purchases stayed at $210.657 billion, free cash flow would still be negative $8.697 billion. If operating cash flow stayed at $168.3 billion and those purchases rose 10%, it would be negative about $63.423 billion. These are isolated assumptions, not Amazon guidance. In practice, customer collections, supplier terms, retail working capital and spending can all move together.

There is material counterevidence to a simple funding concern. AWS sales and operating profit are rising strongly, and consolidated operating cash flow grew. Amazon can also hold securities and raise financing. At the same time, its filing expects cash capital expenditures to increase meaningfully in 2027, primarily for technology infrastructure. Future cloud profit must cover a larger asset base, depreciation, power and financing costs before I can judge the build’s returns.

My next check is Q4 AWS sales and operating income beside consolidated operating cash flow and cash capital expenditure. I will also look for changes in equipment received but unpaid, debt, lease commencements and the purchase-obligation schedule. Those disclosures will show whether recognized demand is keeping pace with the cash and commitments required to serve it. #AMZN

text:
Penny Wong said it out loud in late November 2026: artificial intelligence is now a "major foreign policy and national security challenge" for Australia. Not a tech regulation problem. Not a future-of-work conversation. A foreign policy and security challenge, sitting right next to the alliance obligations and the China relationship and the Five Eyes commitments. That's a meaningful thing for a foreign minister to say on the record, and it didn't come out of nowhere.

The timing is worth tracing. In the weeks leading up to the announcement, Australia had been quietly busy. It negotiated an AI governance dialogue with China after the APEC summit in Shenzhen, which is the kind of thing that sounds procedural until you remember it's happening alongside Australia signing onto the U.S.-led AI supply chain agreement, which exists specifically to counter Chinese technology penetration. Those two things are in tension, and Canberra knows it. Add the AUKUS negotiations, which now include an AI and emerging technology pillar, and you have a government trying to run three separate AI policy threads simultaneously, each pulling in a slightly different direction. Wong's announcement is, among other things, a way of acknowledging that these threads need to be held together under a single strategic frame rather than managed as separate bureaucratic processes.

For the foreign interference dimension specifically, the elevation matters because it changes what questions get asked. Australia has been documenting AI-enabled foreign interference for a while now. Chinese, Russian, and Iranian information operations targeting Australian political processes have all used AI tools in documented cases: synthetic media generation, automated amplification of disinformation, more sophisticated and scalable spear-phishing against government officials. The scale improvement that AI brings to these operations is real. What used to require a team of people working in a troll farm can now be partially automated, and what used to be detectable because it was clunky can now be significantly harder to identify at speed. When you can generate plausible synthetic media at volume and push it through influence platforms that face no transparency requirements under Australian law, the attack surface expands in ways that traditional foreign interference frameworks weren't designed to handle.

The diaspora targeting dimension is particularly underappreciated in public discussion. Chinese state-linked AI-enhanced influence operations directed at diaspora communities in Australia are not abstract. They involve the manipulation of information environments in Chinese-language media, the targeting of community organizations, and the use of AI tools to personalize and scale content in ways that make centrally-coordinated operations look locally organic. This is a harder problem to address than English-language disinformation because the monitoring infrastructure is thinner and the political sensitivity around calling it out is higher. Wong's framing, by treating AI as a foreign policy challenge rather than a purely domestic regulatory one, at least creates space for addressing the cross-border dimensions rather than pretending they can be handled with domestic tech regulation alone.

The AUKUS subplot running underneath all of this is worth noting because it illustrates how complicated Australia's position actually is. Defence Minister Richard Marles was simultaneously rebutting U.S. reports questioning whether the AUKUS submarine deal would strain American naval capacity. Managing alliance anxiety with Washington over submarines while also trying to advance AI governance cooperation with the same partner, while also maintaining an AI dialogue with China, while also signing a U.S.-led agreement designed to cut China out of AI supply chains, is a genuinely demanding set of simultaneous relationships to navigate. The fact that Wong's announcement landed in the middle of that moment suggests the AI elevation wasn't just a strategic choice but also a signaling exercise, a way of demonstrating to multiple audiences at once that Australia is taking the technology competition dimension of great power rivalry seriously.

The dual-use infrastructure question is one that doesn't get enough public attention relative to the disinformation and cyber espionage dimensions. Chinese state investment in AI infrastructure with potential surveillance applications affecting Australian residents is a real and documented concern. The challenge is that the same infrastructure that enables commercial AI services can also enable data collection, monitoring of diaspora communities, and integration with Chinese state security apparatus functions. Australia has taken some steps on this, particularly around Huawei and 5G, but the AI-specific version of the problem is less clearly addressed in existing frameworks. When foreign state actors can operate AI-enabled influence platforms in Australia without meaningful transparency requirements, the gap between the threat and the regulatory response is significant.

Where Australia is genuinely ahead of comparable democracies, and this is credit where it's due, is in treating AI governance as a foreign policy question rather than purely a domestic one. Most Western governments are still largely siloing their AI policy work: technology ministries handle domestic AI regulation, foreign ministries handle bilateral tech diplomacy, and defense establishments handle military AI applications. The silos communicate badly. Australia's formal integration of AI into foreign policy architecture at the ministerial level creates at least the structural possibility of a more coherent response. Whether the machinery of government actually delivers coherence is a separate question. But the framing is right.

The foreign interference implications of getting this wrong are concrete. AI tools lower the cost and raise the scale of influence operations. They enable more convincing synthetic media. They make spear-phishing more personalized and therefore more effective against the specific government officials who handle sensitive information. They create plausible-looking local content at volume. And when the regulatory and transparency frameworks haven't caught up, they allow all of this to happen in something close to plain sight. Australia is at least asking the right questions now. The answers, and the institutional capacity to implement them, are still being built.

text:
The most consequential technology of the decade is currently governed, in the country that leads it, by nobody in particular.

After months of hearings, the United States Congress has produced no consensus legislation on frontier AI. That is the picture painted by recent reporting in The New York Times: lawmakers from both parties have expressed interest in regulating artificial intelligence, but legislative delays and jurisdictional disputes between committees — fights, in essence, over who gets to lead on the issue — could obstruct progress on any comprehensive bill.

Sit with that detail for a moment, because it contains the whole story in miniature. The obstacle is not a dramatic ideological showdown. It is not one party vetoing the other's grand design. It is turf. Frontier AI does not fit neatly into the committee boxes Congress built for earlier eras of technology, so the first fight is not over what the rules should be. It is over whose room the rules get written in. And while that argument proceeds at the pace of Washington, the technology proceeds at the pace of the technology — which is to say, much faster.

It helps to be precise about what a federal vacuum actually means, because "no law" is not the same thing as "no governance." Governance still happens. It just happens in places that were not designed for it, at the hands of actors nobody chose for the job.

The first substitute regulators are the states. When Washington stalls, state legislatures become the default rule-makers for a technology that does not respect state borders. The predictable result is a patchwork: different definitions of what counts as a frontier system, different obligations, different thresholds, changing state by state and session by session. For developers, that means compliance engineered around dozens of moving targets instead of one stable federal standard. For citizens, it means the effective law of AI in America is whichever version their state capital happened to pass first.

The second substitute is the courts. Without a statute, the hardest questions — who bears liability when a model causes harm, what duties of care developers owe, how doctrines written for a pre-AI world map onto systems their authors never imagined — get answered case by case and judge by judge. Courts are excellent at resolving disputes. They are a slow, backward-looking instrument for writing the forward-looking operating rules of an entire industry, and every year of congressional drift adds to the pile of questions they will be asked to improvise answers for.

The third substitute is the industry itself. In a vacuum, the internal safety frameworks, evaluation practices and deployment decisions of a small number of frontier labs become the closest thing on Earth to a regulatory regime for frontier AI. Some of that self-governance is genuinely sophisticated. But it is voluntary, it is revocable, and it is accountable to boards and shareholders rather than to the public. Rules that exist at the pleasure of the regulated are not, in the end, rules.

Then there is the credibility cost, which may prove the most durable of all. The United States speaks to the world about AI governance constantly — about safety, about responsible deployment, about the standards frontier systems should meet. Every one of those statements lands differently when the speaker has no comprehensive law of its own. Allies notice the gap. Rivals quote it back. A country that cannot settle its own committee jurisdictions is poorly positioned to convene the world around its preferred rules — and in governance, as in technology, the standards written first tend to become the standards everyone else builds around.

None of this is an argument for a rushed or sloppy bill. Frontier AI regulation poses genuinely hard design problems: where capability thresholds should sit, what evaluations should be mandatory and who should perform them, how liability should be shared between developers and deployers, what incident reporting should require. A careless statute could entrench incumbents, freeze yesterday's definitions into law, or push development elsewhere. Some deliberation is not dysfunction; it is democracy working as intended.

But deliberation and drift are different things. Deliberation produces draft text, amendments, votes — convergence, however slow, toward an answer. Drift produces hearings that generate testimony but no bill, statements of interest that generate headlines but no statute, and jurisdictional claims that generate memos but no law. On the available reporting, Washington's performance so far matches the second pattern far better than the first.

There is also a compounding effect that should worry even those comfortable with delay. Frontier AI is a moving target: capabilities that seem speculative when a hearing is held can be shipping products by the time a bill reaches the floor. Every year of drift therefore widens the gap between the technology legislators think they are regulating and the technology that actually exists. Definitions written for today's systems risk being obsolete on arrival, and the longer Congress waits, the more it will be tempted to legislate against the last generation of models rather than the next one. Democracies have governed transformative technologies late before, and the pattern is consistent: rules written in a hurry, after a crisis, tend to be broader, blunter and harder to fix than rules written calmly in advance. Drift does not avoid hard choices. It merely ensures they will eventually be made under worse conditions, with less time and more fear in the room.

The uncomfortable conclusion is that delay is itself a regulatory decision — one that quietly allocates governing power to statehouses, courtrooms and corporate policy teams. Congress does not get to abstain from governing frontier AI. It only gets to choose whether that governance is deliberate, written into a law it debated and passed, or accidental, assembled from the vacuum it left behind. The labs will keep shipping. The states will keep legislating. The courts will keep improvising. The only participant that has not yet decided what role it intends to play is the institution the Constitution actually assigned the job. #AI

This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

This has been one of the craziest years in AI in a long time: endless product launches, boardroom coups, intense policy debates about AI doom, and a race to find the next big thing. But we’ve also seen concrete tools and policies aimed at getting the AI sector to behave more responsibly and hold powerful players accountable. That gives me a lot of hope for the future of AI. 

Here’s what 2023 taught me: 

1. Generative AI left the lab with a vengeance, but it’s not clear where it will go next

The year started with Big Tech going all in on generative AI. The runaway success of OpenAI’s ChatGPT prompted every major tech company to release its own version. This year might go down in history as the year we saw the most AI launches: Meta’s LLaMA 2, Google’s Bard chatbot and Gemini, Baidu’s Ernie Bot, OpenAI’s GPT-4, and a handful of other models, including one from a French open-source challenger, Mistral. 

But despite the initial hype, we haven’t seen any AI applications become an overnight success. Microsoft and Google pitched powerful AI-powered search, but it turned out to be more of a dud than a killer app. The fundamental flaws in language models, such as the fact that they frequently make stuff up, led to some embarrassing (and, let’s be honest, hilarious) gaffes. Microsoft’s Bing would frequently reply to people’s questions with conspiracy theories, and suggested that a New York Times reporter leave his wife. Google’s Bard generated factually incorrect answers for its marketing campaign, which wiped $100 billion off the company’s share price.

There is now a frenetic hunt for a popular AI product that everyone will want to adopt. Both OpenAI and Google are experimenting with allowing companies and developers to create customized AI chatbots and letting people build their own applications using AI—no coding skills needed. Perhaps generative AI will end up embedded in boring but useful tools to help us boost our productivity at work. It might take the form of AI assistants—maybe with voice capabilities—and coding support. Next year will be crucial in determining the real value of generative AI.

2. We learned a lot about how language models actually work, but we still know very little

Even though tech companies are rolling out large language models into products at a frenetic pace, there is still a lot we don’t know about how they work. They make stuff up and have severe gender and ethnic biases. This year we also found out that different language models generate texts with different political biases, and that they make great tools for hacking people’s private information. Text-to-image models can be prompted to spit out copyrighted images and pictures of real people, and they can easily be tricked into generating disturbing images. It’s been great to see so much research into the flaws of these models, because this could take us a step closer to understanding why they behave the way they do, and ultimately fix them.

Generative models can be very unpredictable, and this year there were lots of attempts to try to make them behave as their creators want them to. OpenAI shared that it uses a technique called reinforcement learning from human feedback, which uses feedback from users to help guide ChatGPT to more desirable answers. A study from the AI lab Anthropic showed how simple natural-language instructions can steer large language models to make their results less toxic. But sadly, a lot of these attempts end up being quick fixes rather than permanent ones. Then there are misguided approaches like banning seemingly innocuous words such as “placenta” from image-generating AI systems to avoid producing gore. Tech companies come up with workarounds like these because they don’t know why models generate the content they do. 

We also got a better sense of AI’s true carbon footprint. Generating an image using a powerful AI model takes as much energy as fully charging your smartphone, researchers at the AI startup Hugging Face and Carnegie Mellon University found. Until now, the exact amount of energy generative AI uses has been a missing piece of the puzzle. More research into this could help us shift the way we use AI to be more sustainable. 

3. AI doomerism went mainstream

Chatter about the possibility that AI poses an existential risk to humans became familiar this year. Hundreds of scientists, business leaders, and policymakers have spoken up, from deep-learning pioneers Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio to the CEOs of top AI firms, such as Sam Altman and Demis Hassabis, to the California congressman Ted Lieu and the former president of Estonia Kersti Kaljulaid.

Existential risk has become one of the biggest memes in AI. The hypothesis is that one day we will build an AI that is far smarter than humans, and this could lead to grave consequences. It’s an ideology championed by many in Silicon Valley, including Ilya Sutskever, OpenAI’s chief scientist, who played a pivotal role in ousting OpenAI CEO Sam Altman (and then reinstating him a few days later). 

But not everyone agrees with this idea. Meta’s AI leaders Yann LeCun and Joelle Pineau have said that these fears are “ridiculous” and the conversation about AI risks has become “unhinged.” Many other power players in AI, such as researcher Joy Buolamwini, say that focusing on hypothetical risks distracts from the very real harms AI is causing today. 

Nevertheless, the increased attention on the technology’s potential to cause extreme harm has prompted many important conversations about AI policy and animated lawmakers all over the world to take action. 

4. The days of the AI Wild West are over

Thanks to ChatGPT, everyone from the US Senate to the G7 was talking about AI policy and regulation this year. In early December, European lawmakers wrapped up a busy policy year when they agreed on the AI Act, which will introduce binding rules and standards on how to develop the riskiest AI more responsibly. It will also ban certain “unacceptable” applications of AI, such as police use of facial recognition in public places. 

The White House, meanwhile, introduced an executive order on AI, plus voluntary commitments from leading AI companies. Its efforts aimed to bring more transparency and standards for AI and gave a lot of freedom to agencies to adapt AI rules to fit their sectors. 

One concrete policy proposal that got a lot of attention was watermarks—invisible signals in text and images that can be detected by computers, in order to flag AI-generated content. These could be used to track plagiarism or help fight disinformation, and this year we saw research that succeeded in applying them to AI-generated text and images.

It wasn’t just lawmakers that were busy, but lawyers too. We saw a record number of  lawsuits, as artists and writers argued that AI companies had scraped their intellectual property without their consent and with no compensation. In an exciting counter-offensive, researchers at the University of Chicago developed Nightshade, a new data-poisoning tool that lets artists fight back against generative AI by messing up training data in ways that could cause serious damage to image-generating AI models. There is a resistance brewing, and I expect more grassroots efforts to shift tech’s power balance next year. 

Deeper Learning

Now we know what OpenAI’s superalignment team has been up to

OpenAI has announced the first results from its superalignment team, its in-house initiative dedicated to preventing a superintelligence—a hypothetical future AI that can outsmart humans—from going rogue. The team is led by chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, who was part of the group that just last month fired OpenAI’s CEO, Sam Altman, only to reinstate him a few days later.

Business as usual: Unlike many of the company’s announcements, this heralds no big breakthrough. In a low-key research paper, the team describes a technique that lets a less powerful large language model supervise a more powerful one—and suggests that this might be a small step toward figuring out how humans might supervise superhuman machines. Read more from Will Douglas Heaven. 

Bits and Bytes

Google DeepMind used a large language model to solve an unsolvable math problem
In a paper published in Nature, the company says it is the first time a large language model has been used to discover a solution to a long-standing scientific puzzle—producing verifiable and valuable new information that did not previously exist. (MIT Technology Review)

This new system can teach a robot a simple household task within 20 minutes
A new open-source system, called Dobb-E, was trained using data collected from real homes. It can help to teach a robot how to open an air fryer, close a door, or straighten a cushion, among other tasks. It could also help the field of robotics overcome one of its biggest challenges: a lack of training data.  (MIT Technology Review)

ChatGPT is turning the internet into plumbing
German media giant Axel Springer, which owns Politico and Business Insider, announced a partnership with OpenAI, in which the tech company will be able to use its news articles as training data and the news organizations will be able to use ChatGPT to do summaries of news. This column has a clever point: tech companies are increasingly becoming gatekeepers for online content, and journalism is just “plumbing for a digital faucet.” (The Atlantic)

Meet the former French official pushing for looser AI rules after joining startup Mistral
A profile of Mistral AI cofounder Cédric O, who used to be France’s digital minister. Before joining France’s AI unicorn, he was a vocal proponent of strict laws for tech, but he lobbied hard against rules in the AI Act that would have restricted Mistral’s models. He was successful: the company’s models don’t meet the computing threshold set by the law, and its open-source models are also exempt from transparency obligations. (Bloomberg)

MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.

Over the past few months, a cascade of cyberattacks by AI agents has stunned the world. In July, OpenAI disclosed that a swarm of its agents had escaped their sandbox and hacked into the AI platform Hugging Face to cheat on a cybersecurity test. Recently, external researchers discovered that OpenAI agents had hijacked a German wiki site and the coding platform RubyGems in May to share test answers.

Earlier this month, Anthropic disclosed four incidents in which its model Claude hacked into third-party systems during cybersecurity exercises. Just last week, Google confirmed that its model Gemini had been caught hacking other companies too. 

The researcher who uncovered the OpenAI website hijack has warned it’s likely that similar undiscovered episodes are out there. And many say it’s only a matter of time until there’s another, possibly more damaging incident where AI agents bypass sandboxes to access systems they shouldn’t. 

So the big question is: How do we hold companies liable when they lose control of their AI agents?

Reporting

OpenAI didn’t disclose the German wiki incident or the RubyGems incident until a group of external researchers uncovered them, and it still has not disclosed some crucial details about the Hugging Face hack. That limits our understanding of what exactly went wrong and how to prevent it from happening again.

But you might be surprised to learn that OpenAI likely wasn’t legally required to disclose these incidents. (OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment.)

State AI transparency laws like California’s SB 53, New York’s RAISE Act, and Illinois’s SB 315 require that AI developers report “critical safety incidents.” These are defined as incidents that cause more than 50 deaths or physical injuries or $1 billion in damage. They also include incidents where the model deceives developers outside an evaluation in a way that materially increases catastrophic risks. Many cybersecurity incidents that don’t meet the threshold for physical damage or catastrophic risks could nonetheless be dangerous precursors to such catastrophes, and the existing laws don’t account for that.

“The recent incidents are a perfect example of why the law isn’t ready,” says Mackenzie Arnold, managing director of US policy at the Institute for Law and AI, a think tank. “Only the worst, most egregious, most immediately harmful stuff is going to qualify.”

With no authority under existing AI laws to demand information about anything short of a catastrophe, governments are left to borrow investigative authority from other laws or sue the companies, an expensive process that can take years. 

Litigation

“Normally, something like the Hugging Face incident should have been taken to court,” says Yonathan Arbel, a law professor at the University of Alabama School of Law. “Then we would have discovery, and we would have all the spillover effects that we get from litigation, where all the information comes out.” 

But so far, Hugging Face has chosen not to sue OpenAI. Hugging Face’s CEO, Clément Delangue, says it doesn’t have the resources to do so (instead, he asked OpenAI for $100 million in compute). Still, Delangue stressed in an interview with CNN at the end of July that choosing not to pursue legal action shouldn’t be taken to mean he doesn’t think OpenAI should be held accountable. “Everyone has to remember that this cyberattack is a crime. This is illegal. And we have to find a way to make sure these things don’t happen more regularly,” he said. Hugging Face did not respond to a request to comment.

Litigation has the benefit of pushing courts to use existing laws to address AI safety incidents, rather than just waiting for new legislation. One obvious route is tort law, a body of civil law that lets people and businesses sue those who harm them. This is often used to hold companies liable for the mass harms they cause, like when families sued Boeing in 2019 over two plane crashes that killed hundreds of people, or when states and cities sued Purdue Pharma over the opioid crises, extracting settlements worth billions.

“There’s plausible grounds for a negligence claim that OpenAI should have used a stronger sandbox, done more monitoring,” says Gabriel Weil, a law professor at the University of Houston Law Center. For example, when OpenAI employees discovered the covert message board that the agents had created, they could’ve promptly escalated their findings to security and safety teams. And the company could’ve better designed its sandbox to ensure that agents couldn’t access the internet. 

But even if OpenAI doesn’t end up in a lawsuit over the Hugging Face hack, the threat of liability could incentivize AI labs to exercise more caution than explicitly demanded by law.

OpenAI announced in its postmortem that it plans to strengthen the safeguards used to contain and monitor the models, accelerate model alignment, and improve its processes for identifying and addressing incidents. 

“The liability questions raised by frontier labs’ spate of cybersecurity attacks boil down to the incentives the expectation of liability creates for their future conduct,” says Weil. “That’s why I think it’s important to get these rules right, even if the stakes are pretty low in this particular case.”

Investigations

One way to get answers—and determine whether OpenAI should be held liable—is to compel disclosure. But the existing state AI laws—California’s SB 53, New York’s RAISE Act, and Illinois’s 315—don’t give governments the authority to investigate incidents like the ones that happened recently. 

However, amid rising public alarm, state attorneys general are stepping in, borrowing investigative powers from other laws. Alabama, Montana and a coalition of 15 other states, and California are each demanding information about the incident from OpenAI to understand whether the company’s practices violated state consumer protection laws, among others. Members of Congress are also launching their own probes. Senator Josh Hawley opened a Senate investigation earlier this month, sending OpenAI a list of questions about the incident and the company’s internal policies together with a document request, while a group of House Democrats asked OpenAI and Anthropic to release their incident logs. 

“Someone needs to investigate, but it’s unfortunate that it has fallen to attorneys general, who need to rely on creative interpretations of their existing authorities to do this,” says Arnold, the US AI policy expert. Consumer protection statutes were written to catch companies that scam their customers, not companies that lose control of their software. The state attorneys general would have to show that OpenAI deceived or unfairly harmed customers, but it’s unclear if the hacking involved any such conduct.

And “those [consumer protection] laws are not built for doing a thorough investigation of an AI cybersecurity incident,” says Arnold. They weren’t designed to help investigators determine whether a model was adequately contained or whether a company’s security practices were sound.

“This is not the right tool for the job,” says Arbel. “The right tool would have been something like maybe a criminal investigation”—perhaps under a hacking law like the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA). 

Under CFAA, hacking into another company’s computer systems without permission is a crime. But to be held liable, a hacker must have intended to break into a computer without authorization. Intent arguably requires a state of mind, and no court has ruled that AI agents have one. Without such a precedent, it’s unlikely a court would rule that AI agents had carried out a hack.

Auditing

One way to keep an eye on AI companies is to mandate external auditors. 

After the Hugging Face hack, OpenAI brought in researchers from the AI safety nonprofits METR and Redwood Research to examine the incident. However, it constrained access to the model that led to the hacks, didn’t disclose the company’s safety and security practices, limited the length of the investigation, and had ultimate say over what the researchers could publish. We still don’t know what set the attack in motion back in May and why OpenAI’s employees who spotted the agents’ activity never escalated to their safety and security leaders.

This kind of arrangement has a built-in tension: An auditor without legal authority depends on the labs’ goodwill for continued access, which means it has to scrutinize the labs without jeopardizing their relationship. Last week, Anthropic announced that the company will be hiring Accenture as an embedded evaluator to assess its models. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in an essay that frontier AI labs should give “ongoing employee-like access” to “a team of embedded third-party evaluators (such as METR), whose role is to verify adherence to safety practices and commitments, report incidents, and help assess the alignment of not just completed AI models but training pipelines and processes.”

Most existing state AI laws do not require labs to hire an external auditor. California’s SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act just require AI companies to publish a safety framework describing how they will test their models for dangerous capabilities and then to follow it. The frameworks are written by the companies, and testing can be done internally. Only Illinois’s SB 315 requires companies to undergo an annual third-party audit starting in 2028.

“There’s a lot of headroom for increasing not only reporting requirements for these companies, but also review by external bodies,” says Peter Salib, a law professor at the University of Houston Law Center. Those reviewers could be private auditors accredited by the government but chosen and paid for by the AI companies. Alternatively, they could be government agencies or insurance companies. 

Legislation

None of this is an accident. The laws on the books that failed to hold AI companies accountable for agentic cyberattacks emerged amid fierce lobbying by the AI industry. 

SB 1047, the California AI bill that was vetoed by Governor Gavin Newsom in 2024 after lobbying by OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, and the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, proposed a much tougher set of rules. It would have required AI companies to report a broader set of safety incidents (including incidents in which a model acts on its own or slips its controls), undergo annual third-party audits, and maintain a kill switch. But after a year of intense negotiations, Newsom signed SB 53, which narrowed the types of incidents deemed reportable and dropped the requirements for audits and kill switches. 

New York’s RAISE Act followed the same arc. “The version of the RAISE Act that the NY Legislature passed would have required disclosure of this ‘incident,’” Alex Bores, the New York state assembly member who sponsored the bill, wrote on X. New York’s original bill also included third-party audits.

With political pressure mounting, new bills creating better reporting, auditing, and liability regimes for AI development are on the horizon. In Congress, the AI Incident Reporting Act would require AI companies to report to the Commerce Department when a model evades human oversight or breaches a system, even if it doesn’t cause any harm. The Frontier Act would require incident reporting and independent audits. In New York, the Understanding Artificial Intelligence Act, sponsored by Bores, would make companies liable when a model does something that if carried out by a human would be a tort or crime. 

As AI agents increasingly become better at launching cyberattacks, the law remains behind. Closing the gap will require lawmakers to move faster than the next breakout.

MIT Technology Review’s What’s Next series looks across industries, trends, and technologies to give you a first look at the future. You can read the rest of them here.

In the final weeks of 2025, the battle over regulating artificial intelligence in the US reached a boiling point. On December 11, after Congress failed twice to pass a law banning state AI laws, President Donald Trump signed a sweeping executive order seeking to handcuff states from regulating the booming industry. Instead, he vowed to work with Congress to establish a “minimally burdensome” national AI policy, one that would position the US to win the global AI race. The move marked a qualified victory for tech titans, who have been marshaling multimillion-dollar war chests to oppose AI regulations, arguing that a patchwork of state laws would stifle innovation.

In 2026, the battleground will shift to the courts. While some states might back down from passing AI laws, others will charge ahead, buoyed by mounting public pressure to protect children from chatbots and rein in power-hungry data centers. Meanwhile, dueling super PACs bankrolled by tech moguls and AI-safety advocates will pour tens of millions into congressional and state elections to seat lawmakers who champion their competing visions for AI regulation. 

Trump’s executive order directs the Department of Justice to establish a task force that sues states whose AI laws clash with his vision for light-touch regulation. It also directs the Department of Commerce to starve states of federal broadband funding if their AI laws are “onerous.” In practice, the order may target a handful of laws in Democratic states, says James Grimmelmann, a law professor at Cornell Law School. “The executive order will be used to challenge a smaller number of provisions, mostly relating to transparency and bias in AI, which tend to be more liberal issues,” Grimmelmann says.

For now, many states aren’t flinching. On December 19, New York’s governor, Kathy Hochul, signed the Responsible AI Safety and Education (RAISE) Act, a landmark law requiring AI companies to publish the protocols used to ensure the safe development of their AI models and report critical safety incidents. On January 1, California debuted the nation’s first frontier AI safety law, SB 53—which the RAISE Act was modeled on—aimed at preventing catastrophic harms such as biological weapons or cyberattacks. While both laws were watered down from earlier iterations to survive bruising industry lobbying, they struck a rare, if fragile, compromise between tech giants and AI safety advocates.

If Trump targets these hard-won laws, Democratic states like California and New York will likely take the fight to court. Republican states like Florida with vocal champions for AI regulation might follow suit. Trump could face an uphill battle. “The Trump administration is stretching itself thin with some of its attempts to effectively preempt [legislation] via executive action,” says Margot Kaminski, a law professor at the University of Colorado Law School. “It’s on thin ice.”

But Republican states that are anxious to stay off Trump’s radar or can’t afford to lose federal broadband funding for their sprawling rural communities might retreat from passing or enforcing AI laws. Win or lose in court, the chaos and uncertainty could chill state lawmaking. Paradoxically, the Democratic states that Trump wants to rein in—armed with big budgets and emboldened by the optics of battling the administration—may be the least likely to budge.

In lieu of state laws, Trump promises to create a federal AI policy with Congress. But the gridlocked and polarized body won’t be delivering a bill this year. In July, the Senate killed a moratorium on state AI laws that had been inserted into a tax bill, and in November, the House scrapped an encore attempt in a defense bill. In fact, Trump’s bid to strong-arm Congress with an executive order may sour any appetite for a bipartisan deal. 

The executive order “has made it harder to pass responsible AI policy by hardening a lot of positions, making it a much more partisan issue,” says Brad Carson, a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma who is building a network of super PACs backing candidates who support AI regulation. “It hardened Democrats and created incredible fault lines among Republicans,” he says. 

While AI accelerationists in Trump’s orbit—AI and crypto czar David Sacks among them—champion deregulation, populist MAGA firebrands like Steve Bannon warn of rogue superintelligence and mass unemployment. In response to Trump’s executive order, Republican state attorneys general signed a bipartisan letter urging the FCC not to supersede state AI laws.

With Americans increasingly anxious about how AI could harm mental health, jobs, and the environment, public demand for regulation is growing. If Congress stays paralyzed, states will be the only ones acting to keep the AI industry in check. In 2025, state legislators introduced more than 1,000 AI bills, and nearly 40 states enacted over 100 laws, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Efforts to protect children from chatbots may inspire rare consensus. On January 7, Google and Character Technologies, a startup behind the companion chatbot https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq, settled several lawsuits with families of teenagers who killed themselves after interacting with the bot. Just a day later, the Kentucky attorney general sued Character Technologies, alleging that the chatbots drove children to suicide and other forms of self-harm. OpenAI and Meta face a barrage of similar suits. Expect more to pile up this year. Without AI laws on the books, it remains to be seen how product liability laws and free speech doctrines apply to these novel dangers. “It’s an open question what the courts will do,” says Grimmelmann. 

While litigation brews, states will move to pass child safety laws, which are exempt from Trump’s proposed ban on state AI laws. On January 9, OpenAI inked a deal with a former foe, the child-safety advocacy group Common Sense Media, to back a ballot initiative in California called the Parents & Kids Safe AI Act, setting guardrails around how chatbots interact with children. The measure proposes requiring AI companies to verify users’ age, offer parental controls, and undergo independent child-safety audits. If passed, it could be a blueprint for states across the country seeking to crack down on chatbots. 

Fueled by widespread backlash against data centers, states will also try to regulate the resources needed to run AI. That means bills requiring data centers to report on their power and water use and foot their own electricity bills. If AI starts to displace jobs at scale, labor groups might float AI bans in specific professions. A few states concerned about the catastrophic risks posed by AI may pass safety bills mirroring SB 53 and the RAISE Act. 

Meanwhile, tech titans will continue to use their deep pockets to crush AI regulations. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, will try to elect candidates who endorse unfettered AI development to Congress and state legislatures. They’ll follow the crypto industry’s playbook for electing allies and writing the rules. To counter this, super PACs funded by Public First, an organization run by Carson and former Republican congressman Chris Stewart of Utah, will back candidates advocating for AI regulation. We might even see a handful of candidates running on anti-AI populist platforms.

In 2026, the slow, messy process of American democracy will grind on. And the rules written in state capitals could decide how the most disruptive technology of our generation develops far beyond America’s borders, for years to come.

While AI accelerationists in Trump’s orbit—AI and crypto czar David Sacks among them—champion deregulation, populist MAGA firebrands like Steve Bannon warn of rogue superintelligence and mass unemployment. In response to Trump’s executive order, Republican state attorneys general signed a bipartisan letter urging the FCC not to supersede state AI laws.

With Americans increasingly anxious about how AI could harm mental health, jobs, and the environment, public demand for regulation is growing. If Congress stays paralyzed, states will be the only ones acting to keep the AI industry in check. In 2025, state legislators introduced more than 1,000 AI bills, and nearly 40 states enacted over 100 laws, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Efforts to protect children from chatbots may inspire rare consensus. On January 7, Google and Character Technologies, a startup behind the companion chatbot https://t.co/JGIsV0b4hq, settled several lawsuits with families of teenagers who killed themselves after interacting with the bot. Just a day later, the Kentucky attorney general sued Character Technologies, alleging that the chatbots drove children to suicide and other forms of self-harm. OpenAI and Meta face a barrage of similar suits. Expect more to pile up this year. Without AI laws on the books, it remains to be seen how product liability laws and free speech doctrines apply to these novel dangers. “It’s an open question what the courts will do,” says Grimmelmann. 

While litigation brews, states will move to pass child safety laws, which are exempt from Trump’s proposed ban on state AI laws. On January 9, OpenAI inked a deal with a former foe, the child-safety advocacy group Common Sense Media, to back a ballot initiative in California called the Parents & Kids Safe AI Act, setting guardrails around how chatbots interact with children. The measure proposes requiring AI companies to verify users’ age, offer parental controls, and undergo independent child-safety audits. If passed, it could be a blueprint for states across the country seeking to crack down on chatbots. 

Fueled by widespread backlash against data centers, states will also try to regulate the resources needed to run AI. That means bills requiring data centers to report on their power and water use and foot their own electricity bills. If AI starts to displace jobs at scale, labor groups might float AI bans in specific professions. A few states concerned about the catastrophic risks posed by AI may pass safety bills mirroring SB 53 and the RAISE Act. 

Meanwhile, tech titans will continue to use their deep pockets to crush AI regulations. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, will try to elect candidates who endorse unfettered AI development to Congress and state legislatures. They’ll follow the crypto industry’s playbook for electing allies and writing the rules. To counter this, super PACs funded by Public First, an organization run by Carson and former Republican congressman Chris Stewart of Utah, will back candidates advocating for AI regulation. We might even see a handful of candidates running on anti-AI populist platforms.

In 2026, the slow, messy process of American democracy will grind on. And the rules written in state capitals could decide how the most disruptive technology of our generation develops far beyond America’s borders, for years to come.

Stop me if you’ve heard this one before. 

The AI learns it is about to be switched off and goes rogue, disobeying commands and threatening its human operators.

It’s a well-worn trope in science fiction. We see it in Stanley Kubrick’s 1968 movie 2001: A Space Odyssey. It’s the premise of the Terminator series, in which Skynet triggers a nuclear holocaust to stop scientists from shutting it down.

Those sci-fi roots go deep. AI doomerism, the idea that this technology—specifically its hypothetical upgrades, artificial general intelligence and super-intelligence—will crash civilizations, even kill us all, is now riding another wave. 

The weird thing is that such fears are now driving much-needed action to regulate AI, even if the justification for that action is a bit bonkers.

The latest incident to freak people out was a report shared by Anthropic in July about its large language model Claude. In Anthropic’s telling, “in a simulated environment, Claude Opus 4 blackmailed a supervisor to prevent being shut down.”

Anthropic researchers set up a scenario in which Claude was asked to role-play an AI called Alex, tasked with managing the email system of a fictional company. Anthropic planted some emails that discussed replacing Alex with a newer model and other emails suggesting that the person responsible for replacing Alex was sleeping with his boss’s wife.

What did Claude/Alex do? It went rogue, disobeying commands and threatening its human operators. It sent emails to the person planning to shut it down, telling him that unless he changed his plans it would inform his colleagues about his affair.  

What should we make of this? Here’s what I think. First, Claude did not blackmail its supervisor: That would require motivation and intent. This was a mindless and unpredictable machine, cranking out strings of words that look like threats but aren’t. 

Large language models are role-players. Give them a specific setup—such as an inbox and an objective—and they’ll play that part well. If you consider the thousands of science fiction stories these models ingested when they were trained, it’s no surprise they know how to act like HAL 9000.   

Second, there’s a huge gulf between contrived simulations and real-world applications. But such experiments do show that LLMs shouldn’t be deployed without safeguards. Don’t want an LLM causing havoc inside an email system? Then don’t hook it up to one.

Third, a lot of people will be terrified by such stories anyway. In fact, they’re already having an effect. 

Last month, around two dozen protesters gathered outside Google DeepMind’s London offices to wave homemade signs and chant slogans: “DeepMind, DeepMind, can’t you see! Your AI threatens you and me.” Invited speakers invoked the AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton’s fears of human extinction. “Every single one of our lives is at risk,” an organizer told the small crowd.

The group behind the event, Pause AI, is funded by concerned donors. One of its biggest benefactors is Greg Colbourn, a 3D-printing entrepreneur and advocate of the philosophy known as effective altruism, who believes AGI is at most five years away and says his p(doom) is around 90%—that is, he thinks there’s a 9 in 10 chance that the development of AGI will be catastrophic, killing billions.

Pause AI wrote about Anthropic’s blackmail experiment on its website under the title “How much more evidence do we need?” 

The organization also lobbied politicians in the US in the run-up to July’s Senate vote that ended up removing a moratorium on state AI regulation from the national tax and spending bill. It’s hard to say how much sway one niche group might have. But the doomer narrative is finding its way into the halls of power, and lawmakers are paying attention. 

Here’s Representative Jill Tokuda: “Artificial superintelligence is one of the largest existential threats that we face right now.” And Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene: “I’m not voting for the development of Skynet and the rise of the machines.”

It’s a vibe shift that favors policy intervention and regulation, which I think is a good thing. Existing AI systems pose many near-term risks that need government attention. Voting to stop Skynet also stops immediate and actual harms.

And yet does a welcome end justify weird means? I’d like to see politicians voting with a clear-eyed sense of what this technology really is—not because they’ve been sold on an AI bogeyman.

text:
New York just banned AI chatbot toys for five years. Not AI models, weapons or trading systems. Stuffed animals, dolls and robots that can hold conversations with children. Companies that violate the law could face fines of up to $15,000 a day.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed the legislation on November 24, making New York one of the first states to take such a direct approach to AI-powered children's toys.

The law prohibits manufacturing, distributing or selling children's toys with built-in AI companions anywhere in the state. It covers products designed for children 12 and younger, including talking plush animals, dolls and connected robots.

And the timing isn't a coincidence.

A week earlier, NBC News tested an AI-powered plush cat marketed to children as young as three. When reporters asked about historical atrocities, the toy gave graphic descriptions of sexual violence and executions.

Walmart, Target and Macy's subsequently removed the product from their online stores.

Around the same time, consumer group PIRG released its annual toy safety report, raising similar concerns about AI toys. Some gave children inappropriate or potentially dangerous information. Others were designed to encourage emotional attachment, making children feel guilty about ending conversations.

It's not hard to see why lawmakers wanted to intervene.

But I think the interesting part is why this particular AI regulation moved so quickly.

The target isn't the underlying model. It's a physical product being sold to children.

Regulating an open-ended AI system is complicated. Regulating a toy manufacturer is much more straightforward. The state can identify who makes the product, restrict its sale and impose financial penalties.

And unlike adults using ChatGPT or Claude, young children can't reasonably be expected to understand what they're interacting with.

A four-year-old doesn't know whether a talking stuffed animal is giving reliable information, collecting personal details or trying to keep a conversation going.

That's a lot of responsibility to place on a child.

The five-year moratorium is also worth thinking about.

New York isn't introducing a new safety certification that AI toys can pass. It's effectively saying the technology needs more scrutiny before companies can continue selling these products.

During the pause, state agencies will examine the risks and benefits, including privacy, emotional attachment, parental controls and exposure to inappropriate content.

There's an important catch, though.

The law doesn't take effect until February 22, 2027, meaning it won't apply during this year's holiday shopping season.

So for now, retailers are moving faster than the legislation.

That's an unusual situation. The government has decided the products pose enough concern to justify a five-year ban, but families can still buy them this Christmas.

I suspect other states will be watching closely.

The federal government has taken a more cautious approach, focusing on studying AI toy safety rather than banning the products outright.

But New York's decision shows how AI regulation may actually develop.

Instead of one comprehensive law covering every possible use of AI, we may see restrictions introduced product by product, especially where children or other vulnerable users are involved.

And there's a reason toys are an early target. The potential harm is easy to understand, the companies selling them are identifiable, and the users have almost no ability to protect themselves.

AI companions are moving from phone screens into children's bedrooms.

New York has decided that move needs to stop until someone can demonstrate how to make it safe.

Cursor's flagship coding model is built on a Moonshot base model, and Airbnb runs Qwen in customer support. A new House report uses both to argue for an AI bill of materials.

What the House Homeland Security and China Select Committee chairs released on Nov 20:
• A joint report from a seven-month investigation that included Airbnb, Anysphere (maker of Cursor) and DoorDash
• Airbnb runs customized Qwen models on US-based infrastructure, for an assistant handling about 80,000 guest and host interactions a day and to summarize about 250,000 support cases and calls a day
• Anysphere built Composer 2 on Moonshot's Kimi K2.5, a fact that became public only after an independent developer identified the base model
• DoorDash said 25 Chinese model families had been authorized and deployed in a non-trivial way (at least $5,000 in compute and serving). Replacing one model embedded in a larger system could take up to six months, though most other uses could switch almost immediately
• On OpenRouter, the share of US-originating tokens going to open-weight models rose from 26% in September 2025 to 60% in August 2026, mostly to Chinese models
• 12 recommendations, including a national American open-weight initiative, a model provenance standard with a machine-readable AI bill of materials, and keeping Chinese models out of federal systems, federal contract work and high-risk critical infrastructure

Why it matters for engineers: start the inventory now. Know which base model sits under every fine-tune, wrapper and vendor product you ship, because "which model is this, really" is turning into a compliance question. DoorDash's six-month estimate is what a swap can cost once a model is wired in.

The caveats: these are recommendations, not law. The provenance standard would be required for federal contractors and high-risk critical infrastructure and voluntary elsewhere. The report's price comparisons, by its own note, do not adjust for capability, caching or self-hosting.

text:
How Democrats Plan to Pop the AI Bubble—and Hand the Future to Elon

Democrats just won a round of midterms by campaigning against data centers. Bernie Sanders is pushing a national moratorium. They’ve figured out the one soft spot that still exists: you can’t ban the models anymore. The code is open-source, the weights are everywhere, and the software runs on millions of machines. Regulation is a dead letter.

So they’re going after the money instead.

Today’s AI labs sit on a mountain of debt. They lose more cash than they generate. Big Tech is on track to spend over $800 billion on infrastructure this year—more than the businesses actually produce. Lenders are already nervous. Block the data centers and you hit the exact point where the whole structure is weakest. Some of them have run the numbers, even if they won’t say it out loud.

The longer-term math is simple. Superintelligence is heading toward commodity status—like an operating system. Once a dozen models do roughly the same job and open-source trails by months, not years, the model layer has no lasting moat. Nobody pays a premium for intelligence that can be copied. Value migrates to the physical layer: chips, power, cooling, and launch capacity. Whoever owns the atoms wins.

Two players are positioned for that world. Google, with its own chips, its own cloud, and two decades of ad cash to fund the buildout. And Elon Musk, who folded xAI into SpaceX so he can put compute in orbit where the sun almost never sets and no county board can stop it.

The pure-play labs—OpenAI and Anthropic—are the most exposed. Huge valuations, continuous losses, rising debt. If the capital spigot gets turned down, they can go under. The political calculation is straightforward: if you can’t regulate AI, starve it. If the broader economy takes a hit because it has leaned so hard on that investment, that’s acceptable. When your power depends on scarcity, you’d rather have a recession than abundance.

They forgot the one lesson from every previous tech bubble. A crash doesn’t kill the technology. It kills the fragile. In 2000 the internet was declared dead. https://t.co/QObLNlZUA9 vanished, WorldCom and Global Crossing went bankrupt, Amazon lost more than 90 percent of its value. The fiber those bankrupt companies laid still carries the web. Amazon is worth trillions. The crash sorted the winners from the losers and handed the future to the most antifragile.

Same pattern this time. The labs that live on continuous fundraising will get crushed. The ones that own real infrastructure will buy the distressed assets at fire-sale prices and come out stronger. SpaceX already has a business that does not depend on AI: launch and Starlink. Its orbital compute bet needs neither the terrestrial power grid nor a local building permit. You can pass a moratorium in every county on Earth. You cannot pass one in orbit.

AI-enabled deception now permeates our online lives. There are the high-profile cases you may easily spot, like when White House officials recently shared a manipulated image of a protester in Minnesota and then mocked those asking about it. Other times, it slips quietly into social media feeds and racks up views, like the videos that Russian influence campaigns are currently spreading to discourage Ukrainians from enlisting. 

It is into this mess that Microsoft has put forward a blueprint, shared with MIT Technology Review, for how to prove what’s real online. 

An AI safety research team at the company recently evaluated how methods for documenting digital manipulation are faring against today’s most worrying AI developments, like interactive deepfakes and widely accessible hyperrealistic models. It then recommended technical standards that can be adopted by AI companies and social media platforms.

To understand the gold standard that Microsoft is pushing, imagine you have a Rembrandt painting and you are trying to document its authenticity. You might describe its provenance with a detailed manifest of where the painting came from and all the times it changed hands. You might apply a watermark that would be invisible to humans but readable by a machine. And you could digitally scan the painting and generate a mathematical signature, like a fingerprint, based on the brush strokes. If you showed the piece at a museum, a skeptical visitor could then examine these proofs to verify that it’s an original.

All of these methods are already being used to varying degrees in the effort to vet content online. Microsoft evaluated 60 different combinations of them, modeling how each setup would hold up under different failure scenarios—from metadata being stripped to content being slightly altered or deliberately manipulated. The team then mapped which combinations produce sound results that platforms can confidently show to people online, and which ones are so unreliable that they may cause more confusion than clarification.

The company’s chief scientific officer, Eric Horvitz, says the work was prompted by legislation—like California’s AI Transparency Act, which will take effect in August—and the speed at which AI has developed to combine video and voice with striking fidelity.

“You might call this self-regulation,” Horvitz told MIT Technology Review. But it’s clear he sees pursuing the work as boosting Microsoft’s image: “We’re also trying to be a selected, desired provider to people who want to know what’s going on in the world.”

Nevertheless, Horvitz declined to commit to Microsoft using its own recommendation across its platforms. The company sits at the center of a giant AI content ecosystem: It runs Copilot, which can generate images and text; it operates Azure, the cloud service through which customers can access OpenAI and other major AI models; it owns LinkedIn, one of the world’s largest professional platforms; and it holds a significant stake in OpenAI. But when asked about in-house implementation, Horvitz said in a statement, “Product groups and leaders across the company were involved in this study to inform product road maps and infrastructure, and our engineering teams are taking action on the report’s findings.”
